examples.title: A two-year loan with one maturity payment
examples.inputs: $10,000 borrowed, 6% nominal annual interest compounded annually, two years, no intervening payments or fees.
steps: At the end of year one, 10,000 × 1.06 = 10,600. No installment reduces that balance.
This is compounded lump-sum repayment. It is not an interest-only loan with monthly interest payments, or a statement about eligibility for a lender’s deferment program.
examples.answer: Amount due at maturity: $11,236.00; total interest: $1,236.00.

examples.title: Discount the same future payment back to today
examples.inputs: One $11,236 maturity payment after two years, discounted at an assumed 6% annual yield.
steps: The growth factor is 1.06² = 1.1236. Present value is 11,236 / 1.1236 = 10,000.
The $1,236 difference is the discount from the future amount, not a periodic cash coupon.
This mode assumes one maturity payment. Use Bond Calculator for coupons, settlement dates and accrued interest. A mathematical price is not a market quote or a guarantee of repayment.
examples.answer: Bond present value: $10,000.00.

questions.question: How does deferred repayment differ from interest-only repayment?
questions.answer: This Deferred Payment Loan mode makes no interim payments: interest compounds into the amount due at maturity. An interest-only contract instead collects interest during the term and leaves principal for a later payment. The cash-flow timing differs, so the two results should not be compared as the same repayment plan. Contract-specific capitalization, fees and deferment eligibility are not supplied.

loan.scope: Fixed-rate mathematical models: fees, insurance, penalties and lender-specific capitalization rules are excluded. Amortized Loan takes payment and compounding frequencies separately; Deferred Payment Loan assumes no interim payment; Bond Present Value assumes one maturity cash flow without coupons. Enter the actual quote convention. A nominal rate is not necessarily a fee-inclusive APR.
loan.summary: Choose the loan model that matches the payment pattern. Amortized Loan repays principal through regular installments; Deferred Payment Loan compounds unpaid interest into one maturity payment; Bond Present Value discounts a single future maturity amount. A monthly installment, a future lump sum and a present price answer different questions.

examples.title: Solve the monthly payment on a one-year loan
examples.inputs: From the borrower’s perspective: receive $10,000 today; 12 monthly payments; 12% nominal annual rate compounded monthly; ending balance zero.
steps: Monthly rate is 12% / 12 = 1%; N = 12 payment periods, not 12 years.
Payment magnitude = 10,000 × 0.01 / [1 − 1.01^(−12)] = 888.48788678. The borrower pays it out, so PMT is negative.
Twelve unrounded payments total $10,661.85; interest is $661.85 before fees. Round only for display; a lender’s cent-rounded schedule can differ.
examples.answer: PMT: −$888.49 per month. The minus sign denotes a cash outflow.

examples.title: Recover a rate from present and future cash flows
examples.inputs: Invest $1,000 now (PV = −1000), receive $1,210 after two annual periods, no payments in between.
steps: The positive future receipt must offset the negative initial investment: 1,000 × (1 + r)² = 1,210.
r = sqrt(1,210 / 1,000) − 1 = 10% per year with annual compounding.
This is a numerical implied rate under the entered cash flows, not a fee-inclusive regulatory APR or a forecast.
examples.answer: I/Y: 10.00% annually.

examples.title: Solve how many annual periods the same growth needs
examples.inputs: PV = −$1,000; FV = $1,210; 10% annual interest; P/Y = C/Y = 1; PMT = 0.
steps: With no payments, N = ln(1,210 / 1,000) / ln(1.10) = 2.
N is a count of payment periods. Here one period is one year; with P/Y = 12, divide a solved N by twelve to express years.
The constant rate and endpoint values are assumptions. A solver result does not establish when a real investment will reach a goal.
examples.answer: N: 2 annual periods.

examples.title: Find the investment needed for a future receipt
examples.inputs: Receive $1,210 after two years; discount at 10% annually; no intermediate payments.
steps: Present-value magnitude is 1,210 / 1.10² = 1,000.
With the future receipt entered positively, the required investment has the opposite sign: PV = −1,000.
This discounts one lump sum. A stream of payments requires PMT and a consistent beginning/end timing selection.
examples.answer: PV: −$1,000.00, an investment paid out today.

questions.question: Why is the solved loan payment negative?
questions.answer: Signs describe the chosen cash-flow perspective, not whether a number is good or bad. A borrower receiving positive PV repays negative PMT when FV is zero. An investor paying negative PV can receive positive FV. Keep all signs and payment periods consistent; removing a minus sign changes the equation. In the one-year example, negative $888.49 is the monthly outflow before fees.

examples.title: Price a two-year coupon bond below face value
examples.inputs: $1,000 face value, 5% annual coupon, two years, annual payments, assumed 6% annual yield.
steps: The annual coupon is 1,000 × 5% = $50. Cash flows are $50 after year one and $1,050 after year two.
Price = 50 / 1.06 + 1,050 / 1.06² = $981.67. A yield above the coupon rate discounts this bond below its $1,000 face value.
Coupon rate is 5%; current yield is 50 / price, approximately 5.09%; the discount rate used to price every payment is 6%. These are different measures.
examples.answer: Price: $981.67 under the entered cash-flow assumptions.

examples.title: Recover yield from the coupon bond’s unrounded price
examples.inputs: The same annual coupons and two-year maturity, using the unrounded price 981.666073335707.
steps: Solve price = 50 / (1 + y) + 1,050 / (1 + y)² for y.
Using the unrounded price from the preceding example recovers y = 6% annually. A displayed price rounded to cents can imply a slightly different result.
This yield assumes the specified payments occur. Reinvestment, an early sale, fees and default can change realized return.
examples.answer: Yield to maturity: 6.00% with annual coupon frequency.

examples.title: Separate clean price from accrued coupon interest
examples.inputs: $1,000 face, 6% annual coupon, 8% nominal annual yield, semiannual payments; settle April 1, 2026; mature January 1, 2027; use 30/360.
steps: Regular coupon dates are January 1 and July 1. Each coupon is $30. From January 1 to settlement, the stated 30/360 rule counts 90 of 180 days, so accrued interest is 30 × 90/180 = $15.
The next $30 arrives half a coupon period after settlement, followed one period later by $1,030. Dirty price = 30 / 1.04^0.5 + 1,030 / 1.04^1.5 = $1,000.57.
Clean price = dirty price − accrued interest = $985.57. Changing the day-count convention can change both the accrued fraction and price; unusual coupons and ex-coupon rules are not modeled.
examples.answer: Accrued interest: $15.00; clean price: $985.57; dirty price: $1,000.57.

questions.question: Why can settlement-date pricing differ from whole-year pricing?
questions.answer: The whole-year modes discount coupons at full periodic intervals. Settlement-Date Pricing uses the chosen dates and day-count fraction to the next coupon, then separates accrued interest from the discounted payment total. In the April 1 example, 30/360 accrues $15. Clean price excludes that amount; dirty price includes it. Compare the same dates, coupon frequency and price convention before treating a difference as a calculation error.

examples.title: Measure return when another deposit is added later
examples.inputs: Pay $1,000 on January 1, 2025 and $1,100 on January 1, 2026; receive $2,420 on January 1, 2027 as the ending value.
steps: Each interval in this example is exactly 365 days, matching the solver’s date-difference / 365 convention.
At 10%, the first deposit becomes 1,000 × 1.10² = 1,210, and the later deposit becomes 1,100 × 1.10 = 1,210. Together they equal 2,420.
The discounted cash-flow equation is −1,000 − 1,100/1.10 + 2,420/1.10² = 0. Include an ending investment value as a receipt; money still in the account cannot be omitted from the measurement.
examples.answer: Annual money-weighted IRR: 10.00% for these dates and cash flows.

examples.title: Annualize returns from unequal holding periods
examples.inputs: A 10% total return over one year, followed by a 21% total return over two years. Neither row is a deposit or an annual-rate quote.
steps: Total growth factor is 1.10 × 1.21 = 1.331, a 33.1% cumulative return over three years.
Annualized compound return = 1.331^(1/3) − 1 = 10%. Enter the second period as 21%, two years, not 21% for each year.
A simple sum divided by duration gives 31% / 3, about 10.33%; it is not the compound growth rate. Use dated cash flows instead when external deposits or withdrawals matter.
examples.answer: Cumulative return: 33.10%; annualized compound return: 10.00%.

questions.question: Can I compare money-weighted IRR directly with a fund’s reported return?
questions.answer: Not without matching the measurement. Money-weighted IRR depends on your deposit and withdrawal dates and amounts; a fund’s published time-weighted performance measures a different experience. In Dated Cash Flows, include the opening investment and the ending value with consistent signs. The variable-period mode instead compounds entered period returns; it does not remove external cash-flow effects or retrieve a fund’s history.

examples.title: Stock margin: separate position value from your equity
examples.inputs: 100 shares at $50 each; enter a hypothetical initial equity requirement of 50%.
steps: Position value = 100 × 50 = $5,000. Required equity = 5,000 × 50% = $2,500; borrowed amount = $2,500.

As a separate manual stress illustration, a drop to $40 leaves $4,000 of securities against the same $2,500 borrowing: equity is $1,500 before interest and fees. That is a 40% equity loss from a 20% stock-price decline.
The tool calculates the initial position, not this later price path, maintenance equity or a margin-call trigger. The entered 50% is an example, not confirmation of a broker’s requirement.
examples.answer: Required equity: $2,500.00; borrowed amount: $2,500.00.

examples.title: FX margin: keep notional and collateral in the quote currency
examples.inputs: 100,000 base-currency units; 1.10 quote-currency units per base unit; assumed leverage 20:1.
steps: Notional in quote currency = 100,000 × 1.10 = 110,000. Required margin = 110,000 / 20 = 5,500 quote-currency units.

A separate 1% adverse move on that initial notional is about 1,100 quote-currency units, or 20% of the initial margin, before spreads and other charges. This is a risk illustration, not an output forecast.

Collateral is not a maximum-loss limit. Actual permitted leverage, maintenance rules, liquidation and fees depend on the product, jurisdiction and provider; this calculation does not verify eligibility.
examples.answer: Required margin: 5,500.00 in the quote currency, not 5,500 base-currency units.

questions.question: Does required margin tell me the most I could lose?
questions.answer: No. These stock and FX modes calculate initial equity or collateral under an entered assumption, not a loss cap or a maintenance-margin test. Borrowing magnifies gains and losses relative to your equity. Providers can impose different requirements or liquidate positions; losses may exceed the amount initially deposited. Financing charges, changing prices and contract-specific protections are not inferred.

CFTC: OTC forex margin and leverage risks

examples.title: Start with a positive-interest repayment baseline
examples.inputs: Current principal $120,000; 6% nominal annual interest; regular monthly principal-and-interest payment $2,500; no extra payments.
steps: First-month interest = 120,000 × 6% / 12 = $600. The $2,500 payment reduces principal by $1,900, leaving $118,100.
Repeat with each opening balance and cap the final payment at balance plus interest. The baseline takes 56 monthly payments and totals $17,561.33 of interest.
Escrow, insurance, property taxes, daily payoff interest and lender fees are separate. Keep this same balance, rate and regular payment when comparing extras.
examples.answer: Baseline interest: $17,561.33 over 56 payments.

examples.title: Add $250 monthly to the same mortgage
examples.inputs: Use the preceding $120,000 balance, 6% rate and $2,500 regular payment, plus $250 extra principal every month.
steps: First interest is still $600. Paying $2,750 reduces principal by $2,150, leaving $117,850; the lower balance reduces later interest.
The capped-payment schedule takes 50 months, 6 fewer than the baseline. Interest is $15,712.90, saving $1,848.43.
The extra $250 is an ongoing cash commitment. Savings assume the extra reaches principal at the modeled payment time, with no penalty or rate change.
examples.answer: Interest saved versus the same baseline: $1,848.43.

examples.title: Make a one-time $10,000 extra payment in month one
examples.inputs: The same $120,000 mortgage at 6%, $2,500 regular payment; add $10,000 once in month one and no recurring extra.
steps: First-month interest remains $600 because the model charges interest on the opening balance before applying payments. The $12,500 combined payment leaves $108,100 principal.
Later payments return to $2,500. The schedule takes 50 months and incurs $14,605.77 interest, saving $2,955.56 against the baseline.
This uses $10,000 upfront rather than $250 extra each month. The examples have different cash commitments; interest savings alone do not establish which choice is suitable.
examples.answer: Interest saved with the month-one lump sum: $2,955.56.

examples.title: Derive a current balance from original-loan information
examples.inputs: Original principal $120,000; five-year term; 6% annual interest; twelve regular payments already made; no past extras.
steps: Original monthly payment = 120,000 × 0.005 / [1 − 1.005^(−60)] = $2,319.94 before display rounding.
This derives a balance from the original contract assumptions. If you made past extras or have a statement balance, Current balance avoids reconstructing the wrong repayment history.
examples.answer: Estimated current principal: $98,783.62 after twelve scheduled payments.

questions.question: Are the monthly-extra and lump-sum examples equally funded?
questions.answer: No. The illustrated $250 monthly extra and $10,000 month-one lump sum use different amounts and timing. Each is compared with the same original baseline to show the repayment mechanism, not to recommend a winner. To assess alternatives, consider cash available at each date, reserves, penalties and other uses of the money. The tool does not assign a value to keeping liquidity.

examples.title: Compare declining balance with the same straight-line asset
examples.inputs: $50,000 cost, $5,000 salvage, five years, factor 1.5, full years and no whole-dollar rounding.
steps: Annual declining rate = 1.5 / 5 = 30%. Year one expense is $15,000 and book value is $35,000; year two expense is $10,500 and book value is $24,500.
The five expenses are $15,000, $10,500, $7,350, $5,145 and $3,601.50. Total depreciation is $41,596.50; ending book value is $8,403.50.

For the same asset, straight line charges (50,000 − 5,000) / 5 = $9,000 per year and ends at $5,000. This declining model neither switches to straight line nor forces a final write-down, so salvage is a floor rather than a guaranteed final balance.
examples.answer: Ending book value: $8,403.50 under this declining-balance convention.

examples.title: Use sum-of-years digits on the same asset
examples.inputs: The same $50,000 cost, $5,000 salvage and five-year life; full years, no whole-dollar rounding.
steps: Depreciable basis = $45,000; sum of years = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15.
Annual expenses are 45,000 × 5/15 = $15,000, then $12,000, $9,000, $6,000 and $3,000. After two years, accumulated depreciation is $27,000 and book value is $23,000.

Total depreciation reaches $45,000 and ends at $5,000. Different methods change expense timing; none of these book schedules determines a MACRS classification or a tax deduction. Partial-year settings would change the year-by-year allocation.
examples.answer: Total depreciation: $45,000.00; ending book value: $5,000.00.

questions.question: Why can declining balance end above the salvage value?
questions.answer: This implementation applies opening book value × factor / life and prevents the balance from falling below salvage. It does not switch to straight line or force a final write-down. A $50,000 asset with $5,000 salvage, five full years and factor 1.5 ends at $8,403.50. That is a stated modeling convention; your accounting policy or tax rules may require another treatment.

examples.title: Compute a lease payment with interest and a residual
examples.inputs: $30,000 asset value, $10,000 terminal residual, 36 end-of-month payments, 6% nominal annual financing rate.
steps: Monthly rate is 0.5%; annuity present-value factor = [1 − 1.005^(−36)] / 0.005. The residual has present value 10,000 / 1.005^36.
Monthly payment = [30,000 − 10,000 / 1.005^36] / annuity factor = $658.43874903. Total unrounded installments are $23,703.79.

If purchased for the entered residual, total installments plus residual are $33,703.79 before other charges. A residual assumption does not establish that a purchase option exists. The model differs from a dealer money-factor quote.
examples.answer: Monthly payment: $658.44 before taxes and fees.

examples.title: Recover the lease rate from the same payment
examples.inputs: The same asset, residual and 36-month term; enter the unrounded monthly payment 658.438749031114.
steps: The solution is i = 0.005 per month. Nominal annual rate is 12 × 0.5% = 6%; effective annual compounding would instead give (1.005^12 − 1) × 100 ≈ 6.1678%.
A payment rounded to cents can solve to a slightly different rate. Fees and taxes omitted from the cash-flow equation are not converted into a regulatory APR.
examples.answer: Nominal annual rate: 6.00% from the unrounded payment.

questions.question: Why does a rounded monthly payment give a slightly different solved rate?
questions.answer: The rate solver matches the asset value to the payment stream and terminal residual. Rounding the illustrative payment to $658.44 changes that equation slightly, so the recovered rate need not be exactly 6%. Use the unrounded value to reproduce the mathematical example; use actual contractual cash flows to investigate a quote. This nominal financing rate excludes unentered fees and is not a regulatory APR disclosure.
